name: Tacos al Pastor
description: Thin slices of pork marinated in dried chilies, spices, pineapple and achiote, shaved from a vertical spit onto small corn tortillas with onion, cilantro and pineapple. The method is based on the shawarma brought by Lebanese immigrants, and the al pastor taco took shape in Mexico City.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand, topped with salsa and a squeeze of lime.
how_to_order: Ask for 'tacos al pastor con todo' (with everything) at taquerías, mostly at night.

name: Tlacoyo
description: An oval cake of corn masa, most often blue corn, stuffed with beans, fava beans or cheese and toasted or fried. Traditionally eaten with just fresh salsa, it is sold by street vendors, especially in Mexico City.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand or on a paper plate, hot from the comal.
how_to_order: Ask street vendors for a tlacoyo 'de frijol' (beans) or 'de haba' (fava).

name: Chilaquiles
description: Fried tortilla pieces simmered in red or green salsa and topped with cream, cheese and onion, often with eggs or shredded chicken. It is a traditional Mexican breakfast dish.
how_to_eat: Eat with a fork soon after serving, before the chips go soft.
how_to_order: Ask for 'chilaquiles rojos' or 'verdes', 'con huevo' or 'con pollo', at breakfast places and markets.

name: Guajolota
description: A tamal stuffed inside a bolillo or telera bread roll, a cheap, filling snack. It is a street classic of Mexico City, sold near offices, markets and churches and often bought with atole.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand, with atole or champurrado.
how_to_order: Ask tamal vendors for a 'torta de tamal' or 'guajolota' in the morning.

name: Churros con Chocolate
description: Fried ridged sticks of dough rolled in cinnamon sugar, served with thick hot chocolate for dipping. Of Spanish origin, they are a popular sweet across Mexico.
how_to_eat: Dip the churros into the hot chocolate.
how_to_order: Order churros by the piece or bag with a cup of chocolate at churrerías.

name: Pulque
description: A milky, slightly sour alcoholic drink made by fermenting the sap of the maguey plant. Drunk since pre-Hispanic times, it is served in traditional pulquerías in and around Mexico City.
how_to_eat: Drink plain or as a 'curado' blended with fruit or oats.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'curado' (flavoured pulque) or 'natural' at a pulquería.

name: Esquites
description: Corn kernels boiled with epazote, served in a cup with mayonnaise, lime, chili powder and crumbly cheese. It is the cup version of elote, sold by street vendors.
how_to_eat: Eat from the cup with a spoon.
how_to_order: Ask street vendors for esquites 'con todo' (with all toppings).

name: Mole Poblano
description: A dark, rich sauce of dried chilies, chocolate, nuts, seeds, spices and bread, traditionally served over turkey or chicken. It has been called the national dish of Mexico, and legend places its creation in Puebla's Santa Clara convent.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice and tortillas, sprinkled with sesame seeds.
how_to_order: Ask for 'mole poblano con pollo' or 'con guajolote' at fondas in Puebla.

name: Chiles en Nogada
description: Poblano chilies stuffed with a picadillo of meat and fruit, covered in a walnut cream sauce and topped with pomegranate seeds and parsley. Its green, white and red recall the Mexican flag and it is eaten around Independence Day.
how_to_eat: Eat at room temperature with a knife and fork.
how_to_order: Look for it in Puebla in August and the first half of September, when pomegranates are in season.

name: Chalupas Poblanas
description: Small, thin corn tortillas fried and topped with red or green salsa, shredded pork or chicken and chopped onion. They are a specialty of Puebla and south-central Mexico.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand, several at a time.
how_to_order: Order a plate of chalupas, half red and half green salsa, at Puebla food stalls.

name: Cemita
description: A large sandwich on a sesame-seeded roll, filled with meat, sliced avocado, Oaxaca cheese (quesillo), the herb pápalo and chipotle in adobo. Also called cemita poblana, it comes from the city of Puebla.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand; it is big enough for a meal.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'cemita de milanesa' at cemiterías and markets in Puebla.

name: Camotes de Santa Clara
description: Sticks of sweet potato pulp cooked with syrup, often fruit-flavoured, sun-dried and wrapped in waxed paper. Tradition says they were born in Puebla's Santa Clara convent, and they are one of Puebla's famous typical sweets.
how_to_eat: Eat as a sweet snack.
how_to_order: Buy them by the box at candy shops in Puebla.

name: Rompope
description: An eggnog-like drink of eggs, milk, sugar, vanilla and rum or other spirits. It is believed to have first been made in the convents of Puebla.
how_to_eat: Drink chilled in a small glass.
how_to_order: Buy bottles at convents' shops and candy stores in Puebla.

name: Tlayuda
description: A large, crisp toasted corn tortilla spread with asiento (pork lard), refried beans, Oaxaca cheese and vegetables, topped with tasajo, cecina or chorizo. It is regarded as iconic in Oaxacan cuisine, especially around Oaxaca City.
how_to_eat: Eat open-faced or folded in half and grilled, by hand.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'tlayuda con tasajo' at night stalls in Oaxaca City.

name: Mole Negro
description: The best known and most complex of Oaxaca's seven moles, made from six kinds of chilies including chilhuacle, plus chocolate, nuts, seeds, plantain and spices, with several ingredients charred. It is usually served over chicken or turkey.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice and corn tortillas.
how_to_order: Ask for 'mole negro con pollo' at fondas and markets in Oaxaca.

name: Chapulines
description: Grasshoppers toasted on a comal and seasoned with garlic, lime juice, chili and salt. They are most popular in Oaxaca's Central Valleys, where they are sold as a snack.
how_to_eat: Eat by the handful as a snack or in a taco with guacamole.
how_to_order: Buy them by the bag from market vendors in Oaxaca.

name: Tejate
description: A cold, frothy pre-Hispanic drink of maize, cacao, mamey seeds and rosita de cacao flowers. It is sold from large clay bowls in Oaxacan markets.
how_to_eat: Drink cold from a gourd bowl.
how_to_order: Buy a bowl from tejate vendors in Oaxaca's markets.

name: Mezcal
description: A distilled spirit made from roasted agave hearts, giving a smoky flavour. Oaxaca produces most of it and mezcal has Mexican denominación de origen protection.
how_to_eat: Sip slowly, traditionally with orange slices and sal de gusano.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'mezcal joven' or a specific agave such as espadín at mezcalerías.

name: Oaxacan Hot Chocolate
description: Hand-ground cacao combined with almonds, cinnamon and sugar, usually drunk hot, made with water or milk. Oaxaca is famous for its chocolate, served with pan de yema egg-yolk bread.
how_to_eat: Drink hot, dunking pan de yema bread.
how_to_order: Ask for 'chocolate de agua' or 'de leche' at Oaxaca's chocolate mills and markets.

name: Memelas
description: Thick, oval corn cakes toasted on a comal, spread with pork lard and ground beans, then topped with salsa and fresh cheese or quesillo. Dating from pre-Hispanic times, they are typical of Oaxaca, Puebla and neighbouring states.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand, hot from the comal.
how_to_order: Order memelas at Oaxaca market stalls in the morning.

name: Cochinita Pibil
description: Pork marinated in bitter orange and achiote, wrapped in banana leaves and slow-roasted, traditionally in an underground pit (pib). It is the Yucatán's signature dish.
how_to_eat: Eat in tacos or tortas topped with pickled red onion and habanero salsa.
how_to_order: Ask for 'tacos de cochinita' at markets in the morning; it often sells out by noon.

name: Sopa de Lima
description: A soup of chicken, or sometimes pork or beef, flavoured with lime juice and served with crisp tortilla strips. It is considered one of the most representative soups of Yucatán.
how_to_eat: Eat hot from a bowl.
how_to_order: Ask for 'sopa de lima' at Yucatecan restaurants.

name: Papadzules
description: Corn tortillas filled with chopped hard-boiled egg and covered in a pumpkin seed sauce and tomato sauce. Said to be a very ancient Yucatecan dish, it is considered a forerunner of enchiladas.
how_to_eat: Eat with a fork, with habanero salsa if you like heat.
how_to_order: Ask for papadzules at Yucatecan restaurants.

name: Panuchos
description: Fried corn tortillas stuffed with refried black beans and topped with chopped cabbage, pulled chicken or turkey, tomato, avocado and pickled red onion. They are a Yucatecan specialty, mostly eaten in the evening.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand.
how_to_order: Order panuchos in the evening at panucherías.

name: Poc Chuc
description: Pork marinated in citrus and grilled over charcoal. It is one of the signature dishes of the Yucatán, served with pickled onion, rice, beans and avocado.
how_to_eat: Eat with tortillas, pickled onion and habanero salsa.
how_to_order: Ask for 'poc chuc' at Yucatecan restaurants.

name: Marquesita
description: A crisp, rolled crêpe filled with Edam cheese (queso de bola) and sweet fillings such as cajeta, condensed milk, jam or chocolate. Invented in Yucatán in the 1930s, it is sold in squares and parks.
how_to_eat: Eat warm by hand from a paper wrapper.
how_to_order: Buy from marquesita carts in Mérida's squares in the evening.

name: Birria
description: Goat, beef or lamb marinated in an adobo of vinegar, dried chilies, garlic and spices, then cooked in its broth. It began as Jalisco's name for a form of barbacoa and is served in bowls or tacos at birrierías.
how_to_eat: Eat in tacos dipped in the broth (consomé), with onion, cilantro and lime.
how_to_order: Ask for 'birria' or 'tacos de birria con consomé' at birrierías.

name: Torta Ahogada
description: A crusty birote roll filled with shredded pork (carnitas), beans and onion and 'drowned' in a fiery sauce of chile de árbol and vinegar; milder tomato-based versions exist. It is most popular in Guadalajara.
how_to_eat: Eat with your hands or a spoon; it is messy.
how_to_order: Order 'media ahogada' (half drowned) or 'bien ahogada' (fully drowned) at torta stands in Guadalajara.

name: Pozole
description: A hearty soup of hominy corn with pork or chicken, served red, white or green. It dates to pre-Hispanic times and is a festive dish for New Year's Eve, Independence Day and other celebrations.
how_to_eat: Add lettuce or cabbage, radish, onion, oregano, chili and lime, with tostadas on the side.
how_to_order: Ask for 'pozole rojo' at pozolerías.

name: Tequila
description: A spirit distilled from the blue agave plant, mainly in Jalisco around the town of Tequila. It has held a Mexican denominación de origen since 1974.
how_to_eat: Sip neat, often with sangrita on the side.
how_to_order: Ask for a '100% agave' blanco, reposado or añejo.

name: Carne en su Jugo
description: Chopped beef cooked in its own juices with whole beans and pieces of browned bacon. It is a Jalisco specialty, and Guadalajara's Santa Tere neighbourhood is known for it.
how_to_eat: Eat from a bowl topped with onion, cilantro, radish and lime.
how_to_order: Ask for 'carne en su jugo' at restaurants in Guadalajara.

name: Tejuino
description: A cold drink of fermented corn masa and piloncillo, served with lime, salt and shaved ice. It is a popular street drink in Jalisco.
how_to_eat: Drink cold, often with a scoop of lime sorbet.
how_to_order: Buy from tejuino carts in Guadalajara.

name: Carnitas
description: Pork braised and fried slowly in lard until tender and crisp at the edges. Michoacán is famous for them, especially the town of Quiroga.
how_to_eat: Eat in tacos with salsa, onion and cilantro.
how_to_order: Order by the kilo or in tacos, asking for 'maciza' (lean) or 'surtido' (mixed cuts).

name: Carne Asada
description: Beef, usually skirt or flank steak, marinated and grilled, then chopped for tacos. It originated in northern Mexico, where it is a staple and the most common dish at parties and gatherings.
how_to_eat: Eat in flour or corn tortillas with salsa and guacamole.
how_to_order: Ask for 'carne asada' or 'arrachera' at taquerías and grill restaurants.

name: Cabrito
description: Young goat roasted slowly over coals. It is associated with Monterrey and the state of Nuevo León.
how_to_eat: Eat with tortillas, salsa and charro beans.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cabrito al pastor' at restaurants in Monterrey.

name: Machaca
description: Dried, shredded beef, often scrambled with eggs, onion and chili. It is a ranch staple of northern Mexico.
how_to_eat: Eat for breakfast in flour tortillas.
how_to_order: Ask for 'machaca con huevo' at breakfast places in the north.

name: Burrito
description: A flour tortilla wrapped into a sealed cylinder around fillings such as meat or beans. The modern burrito is considered to have taken form in Ciudad Juárez.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand.
how_to_order: Order burritos by filling at stands in Ciudad Juárez and across the north.

name: Caesar Salad
description: Romaine lettuce dressed with olive oil, egg, lime, garlic, Worcestershire sauce and parmesan, with croutons. It was invented in Tijuana in 1924.
how_to_eat: Eat as a starter.
how_to_order: Ask for the salad made tableside at traditional Tijuana restaurants.

name: Aguachile
description: Raw shrimp 'cooked' in lime juice and blended chilies, served with cucumber and red onion. It comes from Sinaloa.
how_to_eat: Eat with tostadas or crackers, very fresh.
how_to_order: Ask for 'aguachile verde' or 'rojo' at mariscos stands.

name: Bacanora
description: An agave spirit made in the Mexican state of Sonora, whose distillation was illegal until 1992. Since 2000 it has had denominación de origen protection, covering agave grown in a set of Sonoran municipalities.
how_to_eat: Sip neat.
how_to_order: Ask for bacanora at bars and shops in Sonora.

name: Huachinango a la Veracruzana
description: Whole red snapper marinated in lime and garlic, then baked in a sauce of tomatoes, onion, garlic, jalapeños, olives and capers. It has been called the signature dish of Veracruz, and its olives and capers show Spanish influence.
how_to_eat: Eat with white rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'huachinango a la veracruzana' at seafood restaurants in Veracruz.

name: Picadas
description: Thick corn tortillas, 8-12 cm across, cooked on a comal and pinched around the edge while hot so the salsa stays in, then topped with salsa, onion and fresh or aged cheese. A cheap, very popular breakfast antojito in the port of Veracruz; unlike a sope, it is griddled rather than fried, though it is sometimes brushed with lard.
how_to_eat: Eat hot by hand, usually for breakfast.
how_to_order: Ask for 'picadas' at breakfast stalls and cafés in the port of Veracruz.

name: Torito
description: A sweet, creamy cocktail of sugar-cane aguardiente mixed with milk and peanut, typical of Veracruz. It began in the early 19th century among sugar-cane workers of the Papaloapan basin, who mixed their aguardiente with seasonal fruit; peanut is the most popular flavour, with fruit versions such as soursop and lime also common.
how_to_eat: Sip slowly; it is strongly alcoholic.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'torito de cacahuate' at bars in Boca del Río or liquor shops in Xico and Coatepec.

name: Arroz a la Tumbada
description: A soupy tomato rice cooked with shrimp, crab, clams, fish and other seafood. It originates in Veracruz.
how_to_eat: Eat from a deep plate with a spoon.
how_to_order: Ask for 'arroz a la tumbada' at seafood restaurants in Veracruz.

name: Zacahuil
description: A giant tamal of coarse masa filled with pork and chili, wrapped in banana leaves and baked in a wood oven. It is from the Huasteca region.
how_to_eat: Eat by the portion with a spoon.
how_to_order: Buy at weekend markets in the Huasteca.
